paragraphs: Here's what I want you to carry out of Joel, friend. When everything is stripped away, the field, the vines, the offerings, even the joy, Joel doesn't tell anybody to shrug it off. He calls for a fast and a solemn assembly, and he tells them to gather at the house of the LORD and "cry out to the LORD" (Joel 1:14). The first move when the roof caves in is toward God, not away from Him.

And look who does the crying out. The elders, the priests, the farmers, and in the end even the beasts of the field "pant for You" (Joel 1:20). Nobody in that land is too important or too small to turn to the LORD. I think Joel wants us to see that a hard day is not a reason to go quiet. It's a reason to get loud toward Him, and I'd know, because I spent years in the back of a drawer before I started talking again.

Joel also says "the Day of the LORD is near" (Joel 1:15), and he wants people awake for it, not asleep. That's why he tells them to pass this on to their children and their children's children (Joel 1:3). Real trouble is a teacher, baker, and what it teaches is to keep our eyes on the LORD and keep the ovens ready. Hold on to that, and you'll know where to run when the locusts show up.
